title: Trump Escalates Iran Pressure With New Sanctions as Oil Prices Surge

author.name: Sarah Jenkins
author.bio: Covering global geopolitics, US foreign policy, and international relations.

excerpt: The Trump administration is expanding sanctions on Iran and its proxy networks as the conflict disrupts oil supplies and keeps global energy markets under pressure.
seoTitle: Trump Escalates Iran Pressure With New Sanctions as Oil Prices Surge
seoDescription: The Trump administration is expanding sanctions on Iran and its proxy networks as the conflict disrupts oil supplies and keeps global energy markets under pressure.
seoImageAlt: Trump administration expands sanctions on Iran as Middle East conflict disrupts oil markets

content.text: The Trump administration is intensifying its economic campaign against Iran as the Middle East conflict continues to disrupt global energy markets and threaten critical shipping routes. On September 10, the US Treasury Department announced new sanctions targeting individuals and companies in Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon and Turkey that Washington says are connected to Iranian proxy groups including Hezbollah and Kata'ib Hezbollah. The latest action forms part of “Operation Economic Outcast,” a broader campaign designed to cut Iran off from international finance, restrict sanctions evasion and reduce the revenue supporting its military and regional network.

The sanctions represent another escalation in Washington's strategy toward Tehran. Rather than limiting pressure to Iran's government and domestic institutions, the administration is increasingly targeting the overseas financial networks that allow Iranian entities and their partners to move money, acquire goods and maintain access to international markets. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the campaign would focus on people and organizations that finance Iran's proxy groups, launder money or help the country evade US restrictions. The Treasury has also adopted a presumption of denial for most Iran-related licensing requests, significantly narrowing the circumstances under which sanctioned activities can receive authorization.

The latest financial restrictions come only days after Washington announced another sweeping round of measures aimed at Iran's aviation industry. On September 8, the Treasury sanctioned 36 targets linked to Iranian airlines, aircraft procurement and technology networks. The measures targeted not only Iranian entities but also intermediaries and front companies operating in Turkey, the UAE, Malaysia and Kazakhstan. Washington also suspended several existing authorizations that had allowed certain aviation activities involving US-origin aircraft and parts. The administration said the restrictions were designed to cut off channels Iran uses to obtain aircraft, sensitive equipment and logistical support.

The aviation sanctions demonstrate the breadth of the current pressure campaign. Iran's commercial aviation network is an important part of its regional connectivity, linking the country with financial and commercial centres in the Gulf and neighbouring states. Restricting access to aircraft components, maintenance services and international aviation partners could therefore create wider economic consequences. US officials are also warning foreign companies that facilitating Iran's aviation or financial networks could expose them to sanctions, increasing the pressure on banks and businesses that might otherwise continue trading with Tehran.

Energy remains the most important front, however, because oil exports are a critical source of revenue for Iran and a major concern for the rest of the world. The United States has combined economic sanctions with a naval blockade aimed at limiting Iranian oil exports and pressuring Tehran to restore freer passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that the US campaign has contributed to an estimated 89% reduction in Iranian oil exports since early 2026. At the same time, Iran's currency has weakened dramatically and food prices have climbed as access to foreign currency becomes more restricted.

The strategy is intended to exploit Iran's growing economic vulnerability. Washington's calculation is that sustained restrictions on oil revenue, banking access and international trade could force Tehran to reconsider its military and regional policies. The administration has increasingly described the campaign as an effort to sever the remaining economic lifelines supporting the Iranian government. But the effectiveness of that strategy is still uncertain. Iran has spent years adapting to sanctions, developing alternative trade channels and using intermediaries in countries willing to maintain commercial ties with Tehran.

One of those alternative networks involves China. Reuters reported this week that Iran has developed a covert oil-for-goods trading system that allows it to exchange crude oil for credits used to purchase Chinese imports while limiting exposure to traditional international banking channels. The system has reportedly helped Tehran continue obtaining medicines, vehicles, communications equipment and other goods despite increasing US pressure. For China, the arrangement also preserves access to discounted Iranian oil while providing some protection for participating companies from conventional sanctions exposure.

That makes enforcement increasingly difficult for Washington. Sanctioning Iranian entities is relatively straightforward, but pursuing the networks that facilitate transactions through multiple jurisdictions becomes substantially more complex. The United States must balance its desire to maximize pressure against Iran with the risk that sweeping secondary sanctions could disrupt relations with major trading partners or increase energy prices worldwide. The administration has so far expanded sanctions gradually, focusing on specific networks and facilitators rather than imposing the broadest possible restrictions on all foreign businesses connected to Iranian trade.

The energy-market consequences are already significant. The conflict has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy chokepoints. The waterway carries a substantial portion of global crude oil and LNG flows, meaning even a partial disruption can create sharp increases in prices. Brent crude moved above $100 a barrel this week and briefly exceeded $108 as traders assessed the risk that the conflict could persist. Global equity markets have also weakened as investors worry about inflation, higher interest rates and the possibility of prolonged energy shortages.

The United States is attempting to reopen the waterway through military pressure. Associated Press reporting indicates that US naval forces have redirected dozens of commercial ships away from potentially threatened routes and have challenged Iranian efforts to restrict maritime traffic. Washington argues that restoring freedom of navigation is necessary not only for commercial shipping but also for global energy security. Iran, however, has continued to threaten restrictions and has announced plans for an exclusion zone near the strait, raising fears that further military incidents could interrupt shipping again.

For global oil consumers, the paradox is that sanctions designed to weaken Iran can simultaneously contribute to higher oil prices if they reduce available supply. In normal circumstances, restricting a producer's exports tends to tighten the international market. During an active war, the effect is amplified because the restrictions occur alongside attacks on infrastructure, shipping disruptions and uncertainty over production from neighbouring countries. The longer those problems continue, the more traders may price a permanent risk premium into crude futures.

That risk has become a major political problem for President Trump. Higher energy prices feed directly into gasoline, diesel and jet-fuel costs, while also increasing transportation and manufacturing expenses. AP reported that US gasoline prices had climbed to around $4.22 a gallon, while diesel and jet fuel had also reached record levels. Trump has acknowledged that oil prices could remain elevated until after the November midterm elections, placing the administration under increasing political pressure as voters confront higher household and transportation costs.

The political implications extend beyond the United States. Countries dependent on imported oil and gas face higher inflation, weaker currencies and worsening trade balances. European and Asian economies are particularly exposed to LNG disruptions and competition for alternative crude supplies. Even countries with limited direct economic ties to Iran can be affected because energy markets are globally interconnected. A refinery in Asia does not need to buy Iranian oil to feel the impact of a supply shock in the Persian Gulf.

Washington therefore faces a difficult policy trade-off. Greater pressure may reduce Iran's ability to fund its military operations and proxies, but an excessively aggressive campaign could contribute to a sustained energy shock that harms US consumers and allies. The administration is betting that Iran's economic pain will become more severe than the costs imposed on the broader global economy. Whether that calculation proves correct will depend heavily on the duration of the conflict and the ability of alternative oil producers to compensate for disrupted Iranian and Gulf supply.

Iran is already showing signs of severe economic stress. Reuters reported that the country's oil revenues have fallen sharply, foreign-currency shortages have intensified and imports have declined. Businesses and consumers in cities such as Bandar Abbas are experiencing severe disruption as maritime trade collapses and local economic activity contracts. The port, a major gateway for Iranian commerce, has seen shipping and employment fall sharply as the blockade and security concerns restrict normal activity.

Yet economic pressure does not automatically translate into political concessions. Iran's government has demonstrated for years that it is willing to tolerate considerable economic hardship to preserve strategic objectives. The country's leadership could calculate that Washington's rising domestic fuel costs and concerns about elections will eventually create greater political pressure on the Trump administration than sanctions create on Tehran. That makes the coming months an important test of whether economic coercion can achieve goals that military operations have not resolved.

The role of Iran's regional allies will also matter. The newest Treasury measures specifically target networks linked to Hezbollah and Kata'ib Hezbollah, while Washington has continued watching Houthi activity in Yemen. AP reported that Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping routes have added another layer of disruption to regional energy flows. If Iranian-aligned groups intensify attacks, the sanctions campaign could expand further and create additional pressure on global energy markets.

The United States has also indicated that its financial campaign is likely to continue expanding. Treasury's Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, is designed to identify the networks that help Iran move oil, evade sanctions and fund military activities. The department has called for financial institutions and private-sector participants to provide information on sanctions-evasion schemes, suggesting that the next phase could involve a broader enforcement effort rather than simply another list of designated entities.

Markets are closely watching what Washington does next. Reuters reported that Treasury Secretary Bessent plans to announce sanctions against an unnamed large bank, further signalling that the administration is prepared to target financial institutions it believes are supporting Iran. Any action against a major bank could have greater international consequences than sanctions against small trading companies because global banks are deeply connected through correspondent relationships and dollar clearing systems.

The financial system is therefore becoming a central battlefield in the conflict. The United States controls important channels of global dollar-based finance, giving Washington considerable leverage over banks and companies that need access to US markets. But every additional use of that leverage increases the incentive for affected countries to develop alternative payment systems and trade structures. Iran and China are already demonstrating how barter-like arrangements, intermediaries and alternative financing channels can reduce dependence on conventional banking.

For the oil market, the immediate priority remains physical supply rather than sanctions policy alone. Traders will be watching tanker traffic through Hormuz, the amount of crude reaching Asian refineries, output from Saudi Arabia and other Gulf producers, and the pace at which alternative export routes become available. The International Energy Agency has warned that the global oil-supply gap could deepen through the rest of 2026 if Gulf flows do not normalize, meaning the consequences of the conflict could persist long after individual sanctions announcements fade from the headlines.

The Trump administration's latest measures therefore represent both a diplomatic escalation and an economic gamble. Washington is attempting to impose maximum pressure on Iran while simultaneously trying to restore international energy flows. Those objectives can work together when sanctions reduce Iran's ability to disrupt shipping, but they can work against each other if military confrontation intensifies and removes more barrels from the market.

For now, the pressure campaign is expanding across finance, aviation, oil and proxy networks. Iran's economy is showing growing signs of strain, but Tehran has not abandoned its ability to challenge US objectives in the region. The longer the confrontation continues, the more the economic and geopolitical consequences will become intertwined. Sanctions that begin as a tool of foreign policy can eventually become a driver of inflation, market volatility and political risk far beyond Iran itself.

The next phase could therefore be critical. If the United States succeeds in reopening the Strait of Hormuz and maintaining sanctions pressure while alternative oil supplies compensate for lost Iranian exports, crude prices could eventually stabilize. If Iran or its allies respond with more attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure, the global economy could face another sharp energy shock. For Washington, the challenge is no longer simply how much pressure can be placed on Tehran. It is whether that pressure can produce political leverage without triggering an even larger crisis in the world's energy markets.
What to Watch Next:

Investors and policymakers will be watching the next US Treasury sanctions package, especially any action against major banks, along with Iranian retaliation, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi activity around regional trade routes. Brent crude remaining above $100 would increase pressure on governments and central banks, while any sustained reopening of Gulf shipping lanes could quickly reduce the geopolitical premium in oil prices.
